title: Wireless Security Foundations
description: Why radio changes the threat model: broadcast medium, no physical boundary, layer-1 evidence, and the legal boundary of testing.
objectives: Explain why 802.11 traffic can be observed without any network access and what that means for a penetration test
Distinguish Wi-Fi (802.11) from other wireless technologies and say why the academy stays focused on 802.11
Describe the engagement lifecycle used by every later module: authorisation → passive observation → test → evidence → next safe decision
State the legal and ethical limits: own lab hardware or a signed authorisation, never third-party networks
artifacts: Lab review: read the sample Rules of Engagement in Engagement Mode and list what is in scope
evidence_focus: Every finding must name the affected BSSID/SSID and the frame or config line that proves it.
retest_focus: A retest needs new evidence from the remediated target and comparable filters; hash each before/after capture separately.

lessons.title: Why wireless changes the threat model

title: Wi-Fi Fundamentals: Identity and Topology
description: SSID vs BSSID vs ESS, BSS/DS topology, bands and channels, and how to read a beacon without guessing.
objectives: Decode a beacon's fixed fields and identify SSID, BSSID, channel, capability and beacon interval
Explain the difference between an ESS, a BSS and a BSSID and why the distinction matters for recon evidence
Map 2.4/5/6 GHz channels, channel width and overlap, and choose a capture channel
Describe what a client leaks in a probe request (PNL, wildcard probes, randomised MAC)
evidence_focus: Extract frame numbers, BSSID, channel and SSID text exactly as captured; keep the capture hash.
retest_focus: Re-run the same tshark filter after a fix so the before/after evidence uses identical extraction.

lessons.title: Identity, topology and reading a beacon

title: 802.11 Frames, IEs and the Association Flow
description: Management/control/data frames, the information elements that carry security policy, and the association state machine.
objectives: Identify frame type/subtype numbers and pick the right display filter for each
Read RSNE fields: version, group cipher, pairwise ciphers, AKM suites and RSN capabilities (including MFPC/MFPR bits)
Walk the association flow and explain what each step proves
Explain what a client must accept for a downgrade to succeed (transition mode, missing PMF, weak AKM)
evidence_focus: Frame numbers + the decoded IE values (not screenshots of text you typed).
retest_focus: Compare the RSNE before and after a configuration change to show the policy actually changed.

lessons.title: Frames, information elements and the association flow
Worked RSN byte decode and evidence decision

title: Monitor Mode and the Wireless Toolchain
description: Interface modes, monitor mode and injection, driver/firmware reality, and choosing the right tool for each job.
objectives: Explain which interface modes are needed for capture vs. injection and why managed mode cannot see other networks' frames
Verify adapter capability (monitor/injection, supported bands) instead of assuming it
Read the regulatory domain with `iw reg get` and understand why setting it is a jurisdiction decision, not a troubleshooting step
Decide when the lab can be completed with a capture (SIMULATION) and when real radio hardware is required (RF_REQUIRED)
artifacts: labs: none (hardware-facing). Uses lab-data summaries to practise interface reasoning.
evidence_focus: Interface name, mode, channel and driver evidence from your own machine (`iw dev`, `iw phy`) when hardware is used.
retest_focus: Repeat the interface check after a driver or mode change and record both outputs.

lessons.title: Monitor mode, injection and the toolchain

title: Passive Reconnaissance and ESS Mapping
description: Enumerate BSSs, clients and relationships from a passive capture, and separate a legitimate ESS from a look-alike.
objectives: Produce an AP inventory (BSSID, SSID, channel, band, security, PMF, WPS) from a capture
Explain why hiding an SSID is not a security control and show the frame that reveals it
Reconstruct client behaviour: what it probes for, where it associates, whether the MAC is randomised
Identify look-alike infrastructure by comparing IE fingerprints, channels and vendor OUIs
evidence_focus: AP inventory table + frame numbers for every claim; capture SHA-256.
retest_focus: Re-run the inventory after remediation and show the look-alike BSSID is gone from the authorised list.

title: Traffic Analysis: From Capture to Evidence
description: Filter, isolate and extract the exact frames that prove a finding — the core skill behind every later technical decision.
objectives: Write display filters that target management subtypes, EAPOL/EAP, RADIUS and BSSID/SSID
Isolate one conversation and reconstruct the association + 4-way handshake with frame numbers
Recognise what is and is not visible on the air (encrypted payload vs. metadata)
Package evidence: capture hash, filter, frame list, and the claim each frame supports
evidence_focus: A reproducible filter string plus frame numbers, capture SHA-256, and a statement of what the evidence does *not* show.
retest_focus: Same filter re-run on the post-fix capture; the delta is the retest evidence.

title: WEP: Why the Design Fails
description: RC4 with a 24-bit IV, CRC32 integrity and why key recovery is a matter of minutes — plus the migration path.
objectives: Explain IV reuse and how FMS/KoreK/PTW recover the key from a capture
Explain why the ICV (CRC32) cannot detect modification
State the correct remediation: remove WEP, do not 'harden' it
Describe what evidence a WEP finding needs (frame counts, key recovery proof)
artifacts: labs: wep-legacy lab notes + generated capture guidance
evidence_focus: IV/frame counts, the recovered key *in the lab only*, and the tool output with parameters.
retest_focus: Post-fix capture shows no WEP BSS and the network no longer accepts WEP association.

title: WPA2: RSN, Handshakes and Offline Audits
description: Understand RSN key setup, read the four-way handshake, then verify only authorized PSK/PMKID fixtures offline.
objectives: Derive PMK/PTK and explain each field the PTK is bound to
Identify M1–M4 in a capture and say what each message proves
Explain why capturing a handshake does not mean the network is compromised
Read RSN capabilities and set/verify PMF (MFPC vs MFPR)
Convert a capture with hcxpcapngtool and run hashcat mode 22000 (unified PMKID + EAPOL)
Compare PMKID collection without a full 4-way handshake (requirements, completeness, station/AP behavior)
Interpret a crack: what access does the key actually grant?
Write the finding with defensible severity derived from impact, not from the technique name
artifacts: labs: wpa2-handshake.pcapng (two clients, one complete exchange)
evidence_focus: The handshake's frame numbers, nonces (first/last bytes are enough), capture hash, and the wordlist/params used.
retest_focus: After a PSK change, the old capture must no longer crack and the new one must.

lessons.title: Handshake evidence: guided and independent decision

title: WPS: The 8-Digit PIN and Its Defences
description: WPS architecture, the 11 000-guess PIN flaw, registrar/setup-locked states, and why disabling WPS beats tuning lockout.
objectives: Decode the WPS IE: version, config methods, device password ID, setup-locked, selected registrar
Explain the 10^7 → ~11 000 reduction and what defeats it (lockout, M4/M6 validation, WPS 2.0)
Explain why 'WPS enabled' is a configuration finding while the PIN attack itself needs an authorization decision
Remediate: disable WPS, or if it must exist, enforce lockout and use PBC with a monitored window
evidence_focus: Beacon frame number, decoded WPS attributes, and AP model/firmware if known.
retest_focus: Post-fix beacon shows no WPS IE (or setup-locked + lockout logs) and a new enumeration attempt fails.

lessons.title: WPS architecture and the PIN flaw

title: WPA3: SAE, Transition Mode and OWE
description: SAE (Dragonfly) handshake properties, forward secrecy, transition-mode downgrade, PMF requirements and OWE.
objectives: Explain why the SAE commit/confirm exchange is not offline-crackable
Detect transition mode from the RSNE (AKM list) and describe the downgrade path
Explain the PMF requirement and OWE's role for open networks
Judge whether a WPA3 deployment is genuinely WPA3-only
evidence_focus: RSNE bytes and frame numbers for the AKM list; a client-side association trace showing which AKM was used.
retest_focus: Re-enumerate the BSS after forcing WPA3-only and verify the PSK AKM is gone.

title: Management Frames, PMF and Look-Alike APs
description: Inspect management-frame protection and same-SSID infrastructure; distinguish frame observations from delivery, ownership and client outcomes.
objectives: Explain why unprotected deauth/disassoc frames can be spoofed and what that achieves
Read MFPC/MFPR from the RSNE and predict whether spoofing will work
Interpret reason codes (1, 7, 8, 15) and SA Query behaviour
Assess availability impact as a finding (and why it is often the weakest but noisiest test)
Compare IE fingerprints, BSSID vendor/OUI, channel, beacon interval and signal to identify a twin
Explain client behaviour that makes evil twin practical (auto-connect, PNL, missing server validation)
Describe detection controls (WIDS/WIPS, authorised-BSSID lists, RF triangulation) and their limits
Design the test safely: which SSIDs are authorised, and what must never be captured from real clients
artifacts: labs: deauth.pcapng (PMF-capable vs PMF-required BSS), wpa3-only.pcapng
evidence_focus: Frame numbers, reason codes, counts and timing; plus client-side evidence (association loss) that the frames had effect.
retest_focus: With ieee80211w=2 the same spoof no longer disconnects the client — capture both states.

title: Captive Portals, Guest Networks and Isolation
description: Portal architecture, session handling weaknesses, and client isolation as a control rather than a checkbox.
objectives: Trace the portal flow (DHCP → DNS/HTTP redirect → portal → session) from a capture
Identify credential exposure when the portal is served over cleartext HTTP
Test whether client isolation is enforced, and explain the difference between isolation and segmentation
Remediate with HTTPS portal, OWE/WPA2-Guest, per-client isolation and VLAN + ACL enforcement
evidence_focus: HTTP request/response frame numbers, session token, and an ARP/ICMP test showing whether peers are reachable.
retest_focus: Isolation enabled: the repeat test shows no client-to-client reachability; capture both states.

title: Enterprise Wi-Fi: 802.1X, EAP and RADIUS
description: Follow the client/AP/AAA trust boundaries from EAP method selection to RADIUS attributes and applied policy; separate the independent synthetic fixtures.
objectives: Draw the 802.1X architecture and name the role of supplicant, authenticator and authentication server
Explain how the MSK becomes the PMK and why the 4-way handshake still happens after EAP succeeds
List the attributes RADIUS returns (VLAN, ACL, session timeout) and the risks of trusting them
Identify the testing decision points for each enterprise component
Identify the EAP method from the outer exchange and explain what is inside the tunnel
Explain MS-CHAPv2 challenge/response and why it is crackable when the server's certificate is not validated
Compare EAP-TLS (mutual certificates) with password-based inner methods
Advise on client configuration: ca_cert, domain_suffix_match/subject_match, and disabling insecure methods server-side
Decode an Access-Request/Challenge/Accept exchange and name the attributes that matter
Verify a Message-Authenticator and a Response Authenticator from a capture
Explain why the shared secret is a high-value credential and how it is attacked (offline guessing against captured authenticators)
Harden: per-AP secrets, require_message_authenticator, source-IP restriction, RadSec, and monitoring
artifacts: labs: radius.pcapng (including a rogue NAS whose Message-Authenticator fails)
evidence_focus: EAP exchange frames, RADIUS code + attributes, and the resulting 4-way handshake — in one timeline.
retest_focus: After remediation, re-capture and show the client can no longer authenticate with the old configuration (e.g. missing certificate validation).

lessons.title: Certificate validation and the PEAP lab

title: Corporate Wireless Kill Chains
description: How individual weaknesses chain into network access: rogue authenticator, credential capture, segmentation bypass — and how each link is broken.
objectives: Assemble a defensible attack chain from the evidence you collected in earlier modules
Test segmentation and isolation with a method whose result is unambiguous (protocol-level reachability, not 'it felt open')
Map each link in the chain to a specific control that breaks it
Report the chain without overstating impact: access to a VLAN is not 'domain admin'
evidence_focus: One timeline: deauth/rogue frames, EAP capture, credential material, and the segmentation test result with frame numbers.
retest_focus: Post-fix: each link is re-tested individually and shown to fail.

title: Wireless Assessment: Scope and Independent Case
description: Plan a bounded assessment and analyze independent synthetic Case C-20 evidence. Northwind remains a planning-only brief; live RF and client outcomes are not supplied.
objectives: Independently inventory C-20 frames, verify fixture handshake inputs and compare staged policy advertisements
Defend each finding against the evidence and remove anything you cannot reproduce
Identify what you did *not* test and why (scope, safety, or environment limits)
Turn a scope document into a test plan with explicit in/out-of-scope artefacts
Apply the evidence standard: reproducibility, integrity (hash), and traceability to a claim
Distinguish tested capture claims from hypotheses and state the next authorized validation test
artifacts: ENG-01: optional written planning scenario; Northwind evidence not supplied
evidence_focus: For each claim cite capture hash, frame and filter; separate observed policy from client behavior and unknown ownership.
retest_focus: The staged beacon shows an advertised-policy change only; live client checks are NOT TESTED.

lessons.title: Methodology, scope and rules of engagement

Separate an exported component from evidence that sensitive data was exposed

objectives: Explain APK/AAB packaging, merged manifest, signatures, resources and DEX without mistaking source excerpts for an APK
Trace untrusted deep-link input through a lookup to an ownership check
Distinguish an interesting entry point from a demonstrated cross-account disclosure

Source clinic: compare an owned demo’s vulnerable and fixed boundaries

title: Exported Components and IPC
description: An exported component is callable only under its installed manifest and permission policy. Trace an untrusted Intent through an entry point to an owned resource before calling it a disclosure.
objectives: An exported component is callable only under its installed manifest and permission policy. Trace an untrusted Intent through an entry point to an owned resource before calling it a disclosure.

Compare a positive (Alice opens note 1), a negative (Alice requests Bob’s note 2) and an unknown ID in both demo flavors. On an owned emulator, record the built manifest, hash, account label and visible result. Without a build, trace the Java branches and mark execution NOT TESTED. The receiver case is source-only: inspect permission protection level and intent reachability before proposing a second-app call.
Never equate exported=true with exploitation. The default Activity lifecycle can reset the mock account; a successful second-app delivery and observed sensitive sink require separate evidence.
artifacts: android-demos/notes-boundary-source.zip (buildable source only; scope limited to mock notes)
evidence_focus: Cite the exact source and SHA-256; separate static reasoning from independently observed device behavior.
retest_focus: A fixed source excerpt is not a retest; run the exact build on an owned emulator with positive and negative controls.

title: Deep Links and App Links
description: Custom schemes route intents without proving domain ownership. HTTPS App Links additionally need an installed manifest, Digital Asset Links and device verification state. Parse scheme, host, path and parameters before any sensitive action.
objectives: Custom schemes route intents without proving domain ownership. HTTPS App Links additionally need an installed manifest, Digital Asset Links and device verification state. Parse scheme, host, path and parameters before any sensitive action.

Make a table of three hosts (trusted.example, attackertrusted.example, trusted.example.attacker.test) and predict the vulnerable and fixed branch for each. A proposed device test needs the exact package/version, resolver state and a controlled destination. For auth redirects, verify a state/nonce and caller trust where applicable; no OAuth exchange is included.
A string comparison alone is not proof of a verified App Link or action execution. Query and fragment parsing, redirects and version-specific resolver state matter; do not invent domain ownership.
artifacts: android-demos/notes-boundary-source.zip (buildable source only; scope limited to mock notes)
evidence_focus: Cite the exact source and SHA-256; separate static reasoning from independently observed device behavior.
retest_focus: A fixed source excerpt is not a retest; run the exact build on an owned emulator with positive and negative controls.

title: Storage, Backup and Data Leakage
description: Map where each sensitive value is created, persisted, rendered and destroyed: app-private files, preferences, databases, cache, notifications, logs, clipboard, backup and shared storage. Android sandboxing and storage protection are different controls.
objectives: Map where each sensitive value is created, persisted, rendered and destroyed: app-private files, preferences, databases, cache, notifications, logs, clipboard, backup and shared storage. Android sandboxing and storage protection are different controls.

List every sink in the example, rank what can be inferred statically, then design an owned-device before/after-logout test with a fake token. Include a positive control that the app still works while signed in, negative control that old data cannot be reused, and screenshot/notification surface check.

Android Keystore makes certain keys non-exportable under conditions, not app-process plaintext inaccessible. Key handling, user authentication policy and hardware backing vary. Do not call an imaginary secureStore secure.

title: Network Trust and Client Sessions
description: Test whether the shipped app validates a server certificate and hostname. Distinguish platform trust, network-security-config, debug overrides, optional pinning and diagnostic interception. A pinning bypass is an observation technique, not a vulnerability result.
objectives: Test whether the shipped app validates a server certificate and hostname. Distinguish platform trust, network-security-config, debug overrides, optional pinning and diagnostic interception. A pinning bypass is an observation technique, not a vulnerability result.

Write a matrix for correct chain/name, wrong CA, wrong name and expired certificate on a future owned test server. Compare exact debug/release builds; record the connected host, OS/API level and selected config. After inspecting traffic, hand off backend authorization claims to the API path.
Do not disable TLS verification on real targets or declare all traffic compromised from seeing a hook/flag. No endpoint or measured request is shipped for this module.

title: WebView and Native Bridge Boundaries
description: WebView creates a boundary between web-origin code and app privileges. Track external Intent data, allowed navigations, redirects, content/file URLs, JavaScript settings and annotated bridge methods before discussing impact.
objectives: WebView creates a boundary between web-origin code and app privileges. Track external Intent data, allowed navigations, redirects, content/file URLs, JavaScript settings and annotated bridge methods before discussing impact.

Trace untrusted URL → loaded origin → bridge method → privileged action, marking missing links. Propose a benign controlled page and a negative origin for an owned demo build. Explain how you would inspect the final origin after redirects and whether an annotated bridge method was actually called.
A URL-filter snippet does not ensure safety across all navigation and API levels. The buildable Notes Boundary project has no WebView; do not claim its APK validates this case.

title: Runtime Observation and Instrumentation
description: A dynamic test combines built artifact identity, controlled accounts, observations and reproducibility. ADB, logs, Frida and debuggers are tools; a hook firing only proves the method executed in an instrumented environment.
objectives: A dynamic test combines built artifact identity, controlled accounts, observations and reproducibility. ADB, logs, Frida and debuggers are tools; a hook firing only proves the method executed in an instrumented environment.

On an owned emulator, launch each flavor, record APK hash/API/account label and observe the positive and negative IDs. Optionally attach instrumentation to corroborate parameter and return values; compare against an uninstrumented run. If no runtime is available, produce a clearly labeled test plan and NOT EXECUTED rows.

Emulators, debugging, instrumentation, lifecycle and anti-tamper can change behavior. Hook success is not a professional exploit or production account leak. No Frida trace is provided or machine graded.

title: Cryptography and Device Identity
description: Test key use, algorithms, IV/nonce generation, lifecycle, keystore protection and biometric/app authorization separately. Device integrity and anti-tamper signals require a server-side decision to affect privileged actions.
objectives: Test key use, algorithms, IV/nonce generation, lifecycle, keystore protection and biometric/app authorization separately. Device integrity and anti-tamper signals require a server-side decision to affect privileged actions.

Design a test with two synthetic plaintexts under one controlled key. Identify the invariant to check (distinct IV per encryption), what your test can infer if the provider rejects a repeat, and a negative control for different keys. Explain why Keystore and biometrics do not automatically enforce server authorization.
Never call a sample key stolen or infer a cryptographic attack from source alone. Provider behavior and actual build data are NOT TESTED.

objectives: Inspect the exact release package and split APKs, manifest, signatures, DEX and native libraries. Distinguish obfuscation as friction from trust enforcement. Dynamic code loading and third-party SDKs extend the attack surface.

title: Independent Android Assessment Case
description: An engagement claim must tie an owned app, a particular installed build and a controlled observation to one trust boundary. Independent practice should also discard unsupported hypotheses; broad tool coverage without evidence is not an assessment.
objectives: An engagement claim must tie an owned app, a particular installed build and a controlled observation to one trust boundary. Independent practice should also discard unsupported hypotheses; broad tool coverage without evidence is not an assessment.

Independently choose two hypotheses from the case pack, build an evidence-gap matrix and discard at least two unsupported impact claims. If you have an owned Android workstation, build and test both Notes Boundary flavors using the project README, with own/other/unknown ID controls, hashes and mock account labels. Without it, submit only a static reasoning exercise and mark the dynamic columns NOT EXECUTED.
Self-review and quizzes cannot certify Android engagement or interview proficiency. Production reports, client sign-off, supervised work and a verified device lab are outside this teaching pack.
